segments.title: The Fog and What It Hides: Bleak House's Opening World

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked — a close reading of what many consider the greatest English novel.
Over the coming episodes, we'll be moving through Dickens' vast, fog-drenched masterpiece — chapter by chapter, image by image, character by glorious character.
Today we begin at the beginning — with the fog, with Chancery, with the world Dickens conjures in those extraordinary opening pages.
I'm joined by three guests who between them know this novel with an intimacy I find genuinely enviable.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who has spent decades reading Dickens against the grain of received opinion.
Edmund believes the novel's power lies not in its politics, but in its moral imagination — in what it asks of individual human character.
Professor James Blackstone brings legal and social history to the table — he knows what Chancery actually was, what it cost, who it destroyed.
When James gets quietly angry about something, you would do well to listen carefully.
And Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, and the voice of more Dickens audiobooks than any living person — approaches the novel as a performer first.
Oliver hears what's on the page in a way the rest of us can only aspire to.
Edmund, James, Oliver — welcome. Let's begin with the fog.
One always feels, returning to the opening of Bleak House, that Dickens has somehow changed the weather of English fiction permanently.
Before those first pages, fog was something that happened to characters. After them, it is a character.
And yet I'd urge some caution against reading the fog purely as a symbol of systemic failure — of capitalism, or bureaucratic oppression, or whatever the current critical fashion requires.
Dickens was, above all, a novelist of the particular.
Consider how perfectly the fog announces itself through individual bewilderment — through Esther's eyes, specifically.
She arrives in London and simply asks whether there is a great fire anywhere.

"He was very obliging, and as he handed me into a fly after superintending the removal of my boxes, I asked him whether there was a great fire anywhere? For the streets were so full of dense brown smoke that scarcely anything was to be seen."
There it is — Esther's guileless question. Not a metaphor. A girl who cannot yet see what she has been brought into.
Edmund is right that Dickens works through the particular — and that's precisely what makes the historical record so illuminating here.
The fog was real. London in the early 1850s burned coal on a scale that made the air genuinely lethal — especially in November, especially near the river.
So when Esther looks out of that fly and sees dense brown smoke, she is describing an actual atmospheric condition that killed several thousand Londoners a year.
Dickens doesn't have to choose between the literal and the symbolic — the literal is already damning enough.
And Chancery itself had a similarly lethal quality — not metaphorically, but materially. Suits in Chancery could run for sixty years.
Jarndyce and Jarndyce was based on a real case — Jennings v. Jennings — which consumed its litigants across three generations.
When Esther asks innocently whether there is a great fire, the irony runs very deep indeed.
There is always a great fire. It simply burns people rather than buildings.
What I love — and I have read that opening chapter aloud more times than I can count — is that Dickens doesn't explain. He accumulates.
Fog everywhere. Fog up the river. Fog down the river. Fog on the Essex marshes. It's almost musical — a ground bass of fog.
And then, buried in all that atmospheric splendour, Dickens slides in a character detail so perfectly observed it almost goes past you.
There's a moment later — and this captures how fog works on character, not just on landscape — when Richard Carstone is in the grip of Vholes.
And Dickens gives him this line — an impatient, self-aware, heartbreaking line.
"I ought to imitate you, in fact, Mr. Vholes?" says Richard, sitting down again with an impatient laugh and beating the devil's tattoo with his boot on the patternless carpet.
"The patternless carpet." That detail. Dickens doesn't say threadbare. He says patternless.
A carpet with no pattern — no design, no future, no readable path. Richard's whole fate is in that word.
And he's beating the devil's tattoo — that old phrase for nervous, purposeless drumming — on it. Magnificent.
Oliver's instinct there is exactly right — and it illustrates precisely why I resist purely sociological readings of this novel.
The fog in Bleak House is not only a critique of institutions. It is a condition of human perception — of what we can and cannot see about ourselves.
Richard cannot see what he is becoming. Lady Dedlock cannot see — or refuses to see — what her past is about to do to her present.
And Esther — our clearest-eyed narrator — asks whether there is a great fire, and is told nothing.
The fog withholds. That is its moral function, quite apart from its atmospheric one.
There is a moment I keep returning to — Esther trying to reach Mrs. Jellyby, which is its own kind of fog, of course.
Mrs. Jellyby, as you'll remember, is devoted to African philanthropy — so entirely devoted that she cannot see anyone actually in the room with her.
And Dickens captures Esther's quiet tactical resourcefulness with characteristic precision.

"As Caddy gave me a glance of entreaty, and as Mrs. Jellyby was looking far away into Africa straight through my bonnet and head, I thought it a good opportunity to come to the subject of my visit and to attract Mrs. Jellyby's attention."
"Straight through my bonnet and head" — that is comic genius, but it is also a serious indictment.
The person immediately in front of you — your daughter, your guest, the poor child on your doorstep — rendered invisible by the grandeur of an abstraction.
Jo, Caddy, Richard — they all suffer a version of this. Nobody quite looks at them directly.
And that's the novel's great structural genius, isn't it — that the fog inside the institutions and the fog inside the characters are the same fog.
Chancery doesn't create obtuse, self-deceiving people. It merely provides ideal conditions for them to thrive.
There's a throwaway line — and Dickens has hundreds of them — that I think about constantly.
The ironmaster Rouncewell — a man of substance and good humour — is asked to confirm something slightly absurd about his brother George.
And Dickens writes, simply: "The ironmaster, repressing his amused smile, assents."
"Repressing his amused smile." Six syllables. An entire character relationship contained in six syllables.
This is what makes reading Dickens aloud such a privilege — the prose rewards the voice the way good music rewards a good instrument.
The fog as moral condition, the fog as institutional critique, the fog as pure literary texture — and all three simultaneously true.
That's rather a good place to have arrived at the end of our first movement.
After the break, we'll move deeper into Bleak House's London — to the characters who live in the fog, and what Dickens does with each of them.
Edmund, James, Oliver — thank you. Stay with us.

segments.title: Suits and Suffering: The Law's Casualty

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens' great novel apart — carefully, lovingly, and with no small amount of argument.
I'm your host, and today we're deep in the machinery of the novel — the courts, the creditors, the casualties.
We're calling this segment Suits and Suffering: The Law's Casualty.
With me today are three people who know Bleak House as well as any novel deserves to be known.
Sir Edmund Leigh — retired Oxford don, lifelong student of Dickens' moral imagination, and a man whose standards for good prose are, frankly, rather terrifying.
Professor James Blackstone — legal historian, specialist in Victorian institutions, and the person who can tell you exactly what Chancery cost in human lives — and precisely how.
And Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, and the man who has read more Dickens aloud than perhaps anyone on earth, which gives him an ear for the prose that the rest of us can only envy.
Today we're looking at a cluster of scenes that circle a single dark centre: the way money, law, and class grind people down — and the strange consolations they find in the grinding.
Edmund, let's start with you — because Dickens gives us, in Mr. Weevle, a figure who seems almost comically insulated from his own misery by fashion.

Yes, and it's a masterstroke of Dickens' satirical economy that he places Weevle — this young man lodging in a dead man's room, above Krook's rag-and-bottle shop — and surrounds him with the gossip columns.
The comedy is in the gap — the absolute chasm — between where Weevle actually is and where his imagination places him.
Dickens tells us, with that wonderful dry relish of his, that to be informed of what the Galaxy Gallery of British Beauty is about —
— is to become acquainted with the most glorious destinies of mankind.
The most glorious destinies of mankind — not Jarndyce and Jarndyce, not the Court of Chancery, not the deaths that litter this novel.
The marriages and rumours of a fashionable gallery.
Dr. Johnson would have recognised this perfectly — the human appetite for elevation by proximity, however imaginary.
And Dickens, unlike some critics I might name, does not despise Weevle for it.
That phrase — 'seems to know the originals, and to be known of them' — has always struck me as extraordinarily poignant, beneath the comedy.
James, from your vantage point, what is Weevle actually escaping from?
He's escaping from the reality of the system that has already swallowed Gridley, that is swallowing Richard Carstone, and that hovers over almost every character in the novel with quiet menace.
Weevle is, of course, Tony Jobling — a Chancery hanger-on, a young man of no prospects waiting, like so many in this world, for something to turn up.
And what strikes me as the historian is this: fashion journalism was genuinely the opiate of the middling sort in the 1850s.
The illustrated papers — the picture galleries — offered precisely the same intoxication of glamour that Weevle is consuming with his borrowed newspaper.
Now consider what sits behind Weevle in this same chapter — Smallweed, Grandfather Smallweed, with his money and his ledgers and his perfectly preserved grievances.
Dickens puts in Smallweed's mouth the most lucid and damning account of Captain Hawdon's debts —
'Didn't he take us all in? Didn't he owe us immense sums, all round?'
The creditor's logic is flawless on its own terms, and Dickens allows it to be flawless — which is far more disturbing than caricature.
That Smallweed passage is one I've read aloud a hundred times, and it never loses its chill.
Because Dickens gives Smallweed this extraordinary quality — the ability to seem reasonable and even jovial while being absolutely pitiless.
'Not, my dear friend,' — and you have to hear how Dickens italicises that 'dear' in performance —
'Not, my dear friend, that I want YOU to betray anything. Far from it.'
That 'Far from it' is a tiny door closing softly in George's face.
Dickens is doing something magnificent with rhythm there — the short sentences tighten like a vice.
Oliver is quite right about the rhythm, and I'd add: the moral horror of Smallweed is inseparable from his comic grotesquerie.
He is a thing from which all warmth has been extinguished — Dickens tells us he has never played, never been a child in any meaningful sense.
And it is precisely this — the death of the inner life — that Dickens places against the sentimental vitality of, say, George Rouncewell or Mrs. Bagnet.
Which brings us, I think, to the Bagnet scene — which is one of Dickens' most underrated pieces of moral writing.
Oh, Mrs. Bagnet — now here is a character who deserves her own novel.
Dickens calls her 'that old girl' with an affection so genuine it almost breaks your heart, coming from a man who was not always kind to the women in his actual life.
But listen to what she actually says to George — because this is Dickens writing for the voice, not the page.
'George, I wonder at you! George, I am ashamed of you! George, I couldn't have believed you would have done it!'
Three repetitions of the name — three blows, perfectly spaced — and the shame accumulates with each one.
And then the ending — 'How could you do it?' — just four words, after all that winding up.
'How could you do it?'
That is a woman, not a rhetorical device — and Dickens knows the difference.
And what makes that scene historically significant as well as dramatically powerful is what it reveals about obligation and honour among the working poor.
The Bagnets — Quebec, Malta, Woolwich — they are not people of means. Their security is relational, not financial.
When Mrs. Bagnet speaks of the 'little moss' for Bagnet and the children to lie upon, she is describing a real and terrible precariousness.
There was no safety net — no welfare state, no recourse to public assistance without the brutal degradation of the workhouse.
So when George compromises their security, even inadvertently, the stakes are not metaphorical — they are existential.
And then we have the passage about Rouncewell's townsman — the ironmaster's connection — which operates on a completely different class register.
This is the scene where the working-class father pulls his daughter away from Lady Dedlock's patronage — and Dickens' framing of it is genuinely startling.
The narrator sets it up with this almost anthropological precision —
'Such was his pride, that he indignantly took her away, as if from reproach and disgrace.'
As if from reproach and disgrace — meaning the act of condescension was itself the disgrace.
'He had no sense of the honour done him and his daughter by the lady's condescension; not the least.'
That 'not the least' — delivered, as Dickens intends, with a kind of incredulous bafflement on the part of the narrator — is the whole English class system in miniature.
I find that passage more complex than Oliver suggests — not that he is wrong, but I think Dickens is genuinely uncertain here, as he rarely is.
The father's pride is presented as admirable — and it is admirable. There is something Burkean in it, actually.
The sense that a man has a station, a dignity, which cannot be amended by another's generosity without his consent.
And yet the daughter loses something — some chance, some connection — and Dickens marks that loss without fully adjudicating it.
Which is, in my view, a sign of genuine novelistic intelligence — not political rectitude, but human complexity.
Edmund's reading is generous to the father, and I understand it — but I'd push back, slightly.
The legal and social historian in me notes that 'condescension' in the Victorian sense was a technical as well as a social term.
For the aristocracy to extend patronage was to assert the naturalness of hierarchy — to say: I can raise you, because it is my right to do so.
The father's refusal is therefore not merely pride — it is a refusal of the entire social grammar that makes such condescension possible.
Rouncewell the ironmaster, of course, enacts the same refusal at Chesney Wold — and Dickens clearly regards him as a figure of the future.

That image of the future — industrial, self-made, resistant to patronage — sits in extraordinary tension with the Weevle we started with, who wants nothing more than to be noticed by a galaxy portrait.
The novel holds both — the aspiring and the refusing — without resolving them.
In our next segment, we'll turn to another kind of casualty — not the man ruined by the courts, but the woman disappeared by respectability.

segments.title: Richard's Fatal Attraction: A Gentleman Undone

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked.
We've spent time in the fog, in the Court of Chancery, in the damp corners of Tom-all-Alone's.
Today we turn to one of the novel's most quietly devastating trajectories — the ruin of Richard Carstone.
With me, as ever, are Sir Edmund Leigh, Oliver Trevelyan, and Professor James Blackstone.
Edmund, let's begin with you — because you've always argued that Richard's destruction is finally a matter of character, not circumstance.
That is precisely my view, and I hold it without apology.
Dickens gives us, in Richard Carstone, a young man of considerable natural gifts — warmth, intelligence, real charm.
What he lacks — fatally — is the discipline to submit those gifts to any sustained endeavour.
Jarndyce v Jarndyce does not create that weakness. It finds it, and it feeds upon it.
Dickens makes this visible in a single extraordinary passage — Vholes and Richard returning to the office after the Long Vacation.

"Mr. Vholes, quiet and unmoved, as a man of so much respectability ought to be, takes off his close black gloves as if he were skinning his hands, lifts off his tight hat as if he were scalping himself, and sits down at his desk."
And then the client — Richard — flings himself into a chair, and Dickens calls him, with devastating precision, "the portrait of young despair."
There it is: the predator composed, the prey collapsed. Vholes does not cause Richard's weakness. He merely profits from it.
I won't entirely disagree with Edmund about character — but I'd push back on what we mean by weakness.
Chancery in Dickens' time was not a neutral arena that tested men's moral fibre.
It was a machine — and I use that word carefully — designed to extract fees from litigants for as long as any assets remained.
The cases that dragged on longest were precisely those where an estate had enough value to sustain the costs — and enough ambiguity to sustain the argument.
Jarndyce v Jarndyce is not a fantastical invention. The real cases were, if anything, worse.
So when Edmund says the suit finds Richard's weakness — yes. But the suit was engineered to find weakness, to create it, to deepen it.
What strikes me in that passage is not merely Richard's despair, but the serpent image Dickens applies to the blue bags.
"Several blue bags hastily stuffed out of all regularity of form, as the larger sort of serpents are in their first gorged state."
Those bags contain Richard's inheritance — consumed, digested, by the system. That is not metaphor decorating a moral failing. That is the diagnosis.
James is right that the system is rapacious — Dickens leaves us no doubt of that.
And yet Jarndyce — old John Jarndyce — is shaped by precisely the same system and emerges from it with his soul intact.
He does so by choosing, with absolute deliberateness, to turn away from it. To refuse engagement. To build his life on other foundations.
Richard has that same choice before him — Jarndyce begs him to make it, repeatedly — and he cannot.
That incapacity is tragic, yes — but it is also moral. Burke would have called it a failure of prudence. Dickens calls it weakness. They are, I think, the same thing.
I love this argument — and I want to live inside it — but can we just sit with that Vholes passage for another moment?
Because what Dickens is doing there is something a novelist can only do — he's giving us two men in a room, and their contrasting physicality tells us everything.
Vholes skinning his hands. Vholes scalping himself. And yet he is the one who is alive.
Richard flings his hat and gloves away — he doesn't even look where they land. That carelessness is the tell.
When you stop caring where your things go, you've stopped caring where you go.
And that brings me to Krook — because Dickens understood that objects hold the story.
There's this extraordinary moment in chapter thirty-two — Weevle describing Krook with his letters, before the spontaneous combustion.
"I heard him a little while afterwards, through the floor here, humming like the wind, the only song he knows — about Bibo, and old Charon, and Bibo being drunk when he died."
Charon. The ferryman of the dead. And Bibo drunk when he crossed. Dickens buries it there like a coal under the floor.
And then Krook goes quiet — quiet as an old rat asleep in his hole. He's already burning. He just doesn't know it yet.
The Krook parallel matters more than it might appear — because Krook is a dark mirror of Chancery itself.
He hoards documents he cannot read. Chancery processes documents it cannot resolve. Both accumulate, and neither dispenses.
And both, in Dickens' vision, combust from within — consuming themselves on the very matter they refused to release.
Which brings me to Esther — and to a passage that's quieter but, I think, just as carefully placed.
There's a moment — chapter forty-five — where Esther blushes.
"I felt the blood rush into my face for the first time, but it was only an instantaneous emotion. I turned my head aside, and it was gone."
That's Esther exercising precisely the self-command that Richard never achieves.
She turns her head aside, and the emotion passes. Richard never turns his head aside. He stares into the suit until it blinds him.
That is a beautiful connection, James. It hadn't quite crystallised for me in that form.
And it points to something Dickens does that's almost musical — he gives his characters contrasting responses to the same kind of pressure.
Then there's George — the other man in this novel who might have gone the way of Richard.
George, who ran from his mother, who felt that shame for decades — and Mrs. Bagnet tells us exactly what he carried.

"When he said at our house to my Woolwich that of all the things my Woolwich could have to think of when he grew to be a man, the comfortablest would be that he had never brought a sorrowful line into his mother's face or turned a hair of her head grey."
He says that to a child. To Woolwich. Because he cannot say it to anyone else.
George is what Richard might have been if he'd had that moral reckoning — the man who knew he had behaved badly, and carried the weight of it, and survived.
Richard never reaches that reckoning. Jarndyce v Jarndyce devours him first.
Oliver has put his finger on something I find deeply moving in the George passages — and I confess I did not expect to be moved by a trooper.
But George is, in a sense, the novel's proof of case for the moral imagination.
He did not behave well. He knows he did not behave well. And that knowledge — unblinking — is what eventually leads him home.
Richard, by contrast, will not look at himself. He looks only at the suit.
There is a wonderful, terrible comedy to the early Richard — we see it even in that offhand moment of Jarndyce laughing about Boythorn's insult.
"Complimentary to our distant relation!" — the exclamation mark doing all the work, Jarndyce delighting in the absurdity.
Richard is there, in that laughter. Young, hopeful, part of the circle. That is what the novel loses.
That sense of what is lost — the Richard who could have been — may be the novel's deepest wound.
Edmund reading character as destiny, James reading the system as trap, Oliver hearing the grief lodged inside the comedy — and somehow all three feel true at once.
That may be Dickens' most remarkable achievement — the case stays open on Richard Carstone long after the last page.
We'll be back after the break.

segments.title: The Gilded Cage: Lady Dedlock's Dangerous Truth

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked — the podcast that takes Dickens' most labyrinthine novel one chamber at a time.
Today we're inside the gilded cage of Chesney Wold — and more particularly, inside the dangerous knowledge that surrounds Lady Dedlock.
The secrets are multiplying, the fog is pressing in, and several characters are beginning to sense that the ground beneath them is not quite solid.
With me, as ever, are Sir Edmund Leigh — whose moral imagination tracks every flaw and every virtue in this cast of thousands.
Professor James Blackstone — legal historian, institutional anatomist, and the man who can tell you exactly what Chancery would have smelled like on a wet Tuesday.
And Oliver Trevelyan — performer, voice artist, and probably the only person alive who has read Dickens aloud more hours than he has slept.
Oliver, I want to start with you — because there's a moment in these chapters that I think is almost entirely about what is not said.
Esther and Charley — and this little window into how Esther reads the people around her.
Yes — and this is one of those passages that a performer falls in love with, because the whole scene is in a single face.
Dickens gives you the setup with extraordinary economy.
"My little maid's face was so eager and her quiet hands were folded so closely in one another as she stood looking at me that I had no great difficulty in reading her thoughts."
Quiet hands folded closely — that is not description, that is acting direction.
Every actor who has ever played a servant trying desperately not to ask for something knows exactly what that gesture looks like.
And Esther — dear Esther — reads it immediately and acts.
No fuss, no performance of virtue, just: we shall go and see what's the matter.
Oliver puts his finger on something rather important there.
Esther's goodness is never announced — it is always enacted.
Which is precisely what separates her from the philanthropists and the committee-sitters with whom this novel is otherwise so richly stocked.
Mrs. Jellyby can save Africa; Esther can read a pair of folded hands.
Now, the contrast with the world of Chesney Wold could hardly be more pointed.
Consider Mr. George's dry remark about provisions — Dickens gives him only four words, but they carry the whole weight of a class system.
"When there is any," says Mr. George — with great expression, as Dickens notes.
The laconic soldier who has seen the underside of England's glorious prosperity — he requires no further elaboration.
And the legal machinery that underpins all of this deprivation is never far from the surface.
There's a moment — one word, really — that I find rather extraordinary in its compression.
Esther, sensing the shape of something menacing circling her, asks simply:
"An enemy?"
That single question tells you that Esther has begun to understand the architecture of danger around her.
In the actual legal world Dickens was writing about, the word enemy would not have been hyperbole.
Chancery had adversaries, investigators, informants — an entire ecosystem of people whose professional interest lay in exposing what others wished buried.
Tulkinghorn is not a grotesque — he is a species of professional that genuinely existed and was genuinely feared.
Tulkinghorn — now there's a performance challenge.
He barely speaks, and when he does the words cost him nothing and cost everyone else everything.
But I want to come back to the emotional undercurrent of these chapters — because there's a passage about Woodcourt that stops me every time I read it.
Esther thinks she has settled her feelings — filed them away tidily, as she files everything.
And then the name is spoken and Dickens gives you this:
"For a moment all that I had had in my mind in connexion with Mr. Woodcourt seemed to come back and confuse me."
Come back and confuse her — not overwhelm, not devastate.
Just confuse — and in that restraint you hear everything Esther will not let herself feel.
That restraint is, I would argue, the very centre of Esther's character — and the most demanding thing Dickens asks a reader to inhabit.
Some readers find her insipid, of course.
Those readers, I suspect, have never met genuine goodness and mistaken it for the absence of passion.
The connexion with Woodcourt is not suppressed — it is sublimated into action, into duty, into those folded quiet hands we began with.
And that sublimation has an institutional dimension as well, which I think gets underplayed.
Esther has no legal standing — no name, no inheritance, no documented identity in any court.
The confusion that washes over her at the mention of Woodcourt is not merely romantic — it is also the confusion of a woman who cannot fully claim her own future.
Because in mid-Victorian England, without a legal identity, your future was largely something that happened to you rather than something you chose.
So the emotional confusions of this section are never purely personal — they are always already shadowed by legal and social realities pressing in from every side.
We began with folded hands and a single eager face — and we have arrived, as Dickens always arranges it, at the machinery of an entire society.
When we return, we'll move deeper into Chesney Wold — and ask what Lady Dedlock's secret is actually threatening to destroy.

segments.title: Bleak Houses and Bitter Laughter: Comedy in Dickens's Darkest Work

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked — the podcast that takes Dickens's longest, strangest, and arguably greatest novel seriously, one chapter at a time.
Today we're taking on a question that sounds almost paradoxical: the comedy in Bleak House.
Because this is, after all, a novel about a lawsuit that destroys everyone it touches, a spontaneous combustion, a crossing-sweeper who dies in the gutter.
And yet Dickens is funny here — devastatingly, structurally, sometimes savagely funny.
To explore that tension, I have three guides with me, and I couldn't ask for better ones.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don whose devotion to Dickens is matched only by his suspicion of people who read Dickens for the wrong reasons.
Edmund, welcome.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal historian who has spent a career understanding exactly what Chancery was and exactly how it crushed people — which makes him indispensable here.
James, good to have you.
And Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, and the man who has read more Dickens aloud than perhaps anyone alive — brings the performer's ear to the text.
Oliver, always a pleasure.
Let's begin with the question itself: can a novel this dark support genuine comedy — or is the laughter always a little sick?
The question contains its own answer, I think.
Dickens understood — as Shakespeare understood before him — that comedy and tragedy are not opposites.
They are, rather, two instruments playing the same chord.
The Chancery grotesques — Vholes, Krook, the Smallweeds — are genuinely hilarious figures.
But the laughter they provoke is the laughter of recognition — and recognition, in this novel, is always attended by dread.
Burke wrote that the sublime and the beautiful cannot coexist in a single object.
Dickens spent his entire career proving Burke wrong.
Edmund, I'd go further.
I think Dickens is actually funnier in Bleak House than almost anywhere else precisely because the stakes are so unbearably high.
Take Bucket.
Here is Dickens describing a detective who is essentially omniscient, morally ambiguous, potentially dangerous — and the prose renders him as a kind of benign flaneur.
Listen to the setup:
"Otherwise mildly studious in his observation of human nature, on the whole a benignant philosopher not disposed to be severe upon the follies of mankind."
You're nodding along, almost charmed — and then Dickens drops the blade:
"but through the placid stream of his life there glides an under-current of forefinger."
That final word — forefinger — is a joke and a threat simultaneously.
That is Dickens at full stretch — the comedy and the menace arriving in the same syllable.
Oliver's chosen a fascinating example, because Bucket is the one character in the novel who moves freely across every social stratum.
He drinks with the poor, advises the aristocracy, and manipulates everyone in between.
The comedy in his portrait isn't incidental — it's the mechanism of his power.
If I want to show you something truly chilling in the comic register, I'd direct you to Vholes.
Dickens gives him this extraordinary speech — absolutely straight-faced, impeccably professional — and every syllable is an act of predation.
Vholes is setting out his ethical credentials, naming his daughters — Emma, Jane, and Caroline — as though invoking saints.
"Those interests are now paramount in this office.
My digestive functions, as you may have heard me mention, are not in a good state, and rest might improve them; but I shall not rest, sir, while I am your representative."
His digestive functions.
Dickens has him invoke his dyspepsia as a form of professional sacrifice — and it is both perfectly absurd and perfectly accurate to how self-interested people speak.
I've sat in courtrooms with men who sounded exactly like that.
James puts his finger on something essential about the Vholes passage.
The comedy in Vholes is the comedy of moral camouflage — language deployed with complete grammatical propriety in the service of complete ethical vacancy.
And Richard Carstone is destroyed by it — not because he is a fool, but because he is young, and hope is a vulnerability.
There is a later moment, almost unbearably spare, where Richard is asked how the world fares, and he says:
"Badly enough, and slowly enough — speaking at least for my part of it."
Eight words of comedy — and also eight words of a young man's epitaph.
That is where Dickens surpasses himself: when the joke and the elegy are indistinguishable.
Edmund, that line from Richard — I have read it aloud perhaps a dozen times and it still stops me.
Because on the page it looks almost throwaway — a shrug, a bit of sardonic chat.
But said aloud, with Richard's exhaustion behind it, it's devastating.
This is the great discovery you make performing Dickens: the comic lines and the tragic lines are often the same lines.
The delivery — the pause, the weight you put behind a word — is the difference between a laugh and a silence.
I want to bring in one more passage, because it sits at an angle to everything we've been saying.
When George Rouncewell is finally reunited with his mother, Dickens writes something that refuses comedy entirely.
The trooper — this soldier who has been armoured in self-sufficiency the entire novel — simply breaks.
"He puts his hands together as a child does when it says its prayers, and raising them towards her breast, bows down his head, and cries."
What interests me is what this scene tells us about the novel's comedy by contrast.
Dickens earns these moments of pure, unironic tenderness precisely because he has been so savage everywhere else.
The satire of Vholes and the grief of George Rouncewell are not in competition.
They require each other.
That is elegantly put, James, and I think it goes to the heart of why this novel endures.
A novelist who gave us only the Vholes comedy would be a great satirist.
A novelist who gave us only George at his mother's feet would be a great sentimentalist.
Dickens gives us both on consecutive pages — and neither cancels the other out.
That is not craft. That is genius.
Comedy as the structural condition for tragedy — and tragedy as what gives the comedy its edge.
Vholes and his digestive functions, Bucket and his forefinger, Richard's bleak little shrug, George weeping like a child.
All Dickens. All the same novel.
We'll take a short break and return to look more closely at the characters who carry the novel's satirical weight — and what Dickens is really asking us to laugh at.

segments.title: Connected Fates: How Dickens Weaves His Web

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked.
We've been talking about how Dickens holds this vast, crowded novel together — and today we're asking a more particular question.
Not just the famous fog, or the Court of Chancery at the centre — but the smaller connective tissue.
The moment a character is observed by another who doesn't quite know what they're seeing.
Sir Edmund Leigh is with us — retired Oxford don and a reader who insists on the primacy of individual character over social thesis.
Edmund, you've been circling a moment involving Mrs. Bagnet and George.
Yes — and it is, on the surface, a thoroughly unremarkable moment.
Mrs. Bagnet is a practical woman, not a subtle one — and yet Dickens gives her this quiet, precise observation about George.
She says, and I want to read it exactly as it stands:
Now — freedom is the word she reaches for first when she wants to defend him.
"Of course he must be free or he wouldn't be George."
That is a woman defining a man's soul in a single clause.
And yet the very next breath — "he smarts and seems put out."
There is something chafing against that freedom, and she cannot name it — but she feels it.
What's pressing on George at that point in the novel is, of course, the shadow of Tulkinghorn's murder — and a legal system entirely indifferent to the distinction between guilt and innocence.
Mrs. Bagnet reads restlessness in his body without knowing the cause.
That gap — between what a witness observes and what is actually at stake — is very Dickensian, and very true to how institutions operate.
There's also something worth noting about George himself — when we first see him in Chapter Twenty-four, he tells us exactly who he is.
He is asked about his punctuality, and his answer is a small masterpiece of self-definition:
He knows himself completely — and that self-knowledge is both his strength and, eventually, his trap.
A man shaped entirely by military discipline, suddenly dropped into a world governed by lawyers.
That contrast is essential, and I think it's where Dickens' moral imagination is at its most precise.
George's virtue is a soldier's virtue — loyalty, punctuality, directness.
None of those qualities are remotely legible to Chancery.
Which is precisely why Dickens chose him as his figure of threatened innocence, rather than some more obviously pitiable wretch.
And that line — "I am not at all business-like" — is funnier and sadder than it has any right to be.
He says it with complete equanimity, as though "not business-like" is simply a fact about himself, like being left-handed.
He has no idea that the entire novel is about to make that quality matter enormously.
Now — Mrs. Rouncewell and Lady Dedlock, that is a rather different kind of observation scene, isn't it?
Dickens is doing something wonderfully sly there with Rosa's raptures.
"She is so affable, so graceful, so beautiful, so elegant" — it's practically a parody of devotion.
And then Mrs. Rouncewell arrives like a slow, courteous correction.
That scene rewards very close reading, because the comedy is also, I think, a form of tragedy in miniature.
Mrs. Rouncewell has served the Dedlocks all her life, and her loyalty is genuine and unshakeable.
And yet she cannot quite bring herself to endorse Rosa's uncritical worship.
Listen to how Dickens threads the needle here — this is Mrs. Rouncewell's careful qualification:
The phrase "a little more free" is exquisite — it echoes Mrs. Bagnet on George almost exactly.
Freedom, warmth, approachability — these are the human qualities this novel keeps measuring its characters against.
And Lady Dedlock cannot be free — that is the whole point.
She is imprisoned by her secret, by her class, by the sheer performance of aristocratic composure that her position demands.
Mrs. Rouncewell reads coldness where there is, in fact, terror.
That is exactly the kind of observational irony Dickens deploys again and again — a witness who is right about the symptom and entirely wrong about the disease.
"Heaven forbid that she should say a syllable in dispraise" — and then she proceeds to do precisely that, in the most gracious possible way.
It is a perfect piece of English social comedy — the polite negative so elaborately constructed that it becomes its own form of criticism.
Dickens must have heard that exact tone a thousand times in drawing rooms and back parlours.
And — briefly — there's the tiny cameo of Guppy spotting Jobling and Small nodding from the window.
"Small's head looks out of window too and nods to Jobling."
Just a head, popping out and nodding.
Smallweed is barely human at the best of times — Dickens reduces him to a head and a nod and it's completely right.
The nod from the window — and yet somehow it lands.
What strikes me across all of these moments is that Dickens is constantly giving us witnesses — characters who see, but only partially.
Mrs. Bagnet reads George's body; Mrs. Rouncewell reads Lady Dedlock's manner; Guppy reads Jobling's presence in the street.
None of them has the full picture — and neither, for a long time, do we.
We'll be turning to one of the novel's great set-pieces next — and asking what it means that Dickens chose to give us two narrators rather than one.

segments.title: The Weight of Secrets: What Bleak House Endures

utterances.text: We come now to our closing segment — and in a novel as vast and intricate as Bleak House, endings feel both inevitable and earned.
We've spent time today with fog and fire, with courts and the crossing-sweeper who doesn't know the alphabet.
But I want to end where Dickens always returns: to the question of what endures.
What survives Chancery, secrets, self-deception, the long slow corruption of institutions?
Edmund, I'd like to begin with you — and with a scene that might seem, at first glance, merely comic.
The inquest at Krook's, the beadle in his glory, the journalists with their special little table.
What does Dickens give us there, beneath the satire?
The scene is, on its surface, a perfectly calibrated piece of Dickensian grotesque.
The jury inspect the body — some of them retreating pale and precipitately, as Dickens notes — while the real theatre of the moment belongs to the beadle.
Dickens gives us the man's inner life with devastating economy.
He is, Dickens tells us, setting up that magnificent passage about the reporters —
"not superior to the universal human infirmity, but hopes to read in print what 'Mooney, the active and intelligent beadle of the district,' said and did."
The universal human infirmity — vanity, the craving to be seen, to be named.
Dickens locates it not in a villain but in a minor functionary hoping for a line in the newspaper.
That is precisely where moral imagination operates at its most devastating — in the utterly ordinary.
What strikes me every time I read that passage aloud is the rhythm of the man's ambition.
Dickens builds it in rising clauses — said and did, and even aspires.
And then that final perfect stroke — as familiarly and patronizingly mentioned as the name of the hangman.
The beadle's ceiling of aspiration is to be as notorious as the public executioner.
It's absurd, it's exact, and it lands like a closed trap.
Edmund is right — it's the ordinariness that makes it sting.
But I'd add: Dickens is also writing about the press, about the machinery by which events become stories — and stories become power.
Oliver puts his finger on something the historical record confirms with some force.
Victorian coroner's inquests were genuinely porous events — the press attended as a matter of course, and the beadle's relationship with local reporters was not merely satirical invention.
The point Dickens is making is one about institutional complicity — about how systems perpetuate themselves through the vanity of their servants.
Everyone in that room wants a mention — and so no one asks the harder question about the body.
And yet I would resist the temptation to make it purely systemic.
The beadle is not a function — he is a character with a name, a hunger, a small and rather touching aspiration.
Mooney wants to matter.
That is a moral fact about a person before it is a critique of a structure.
Burke would say — and Dickens I think would agree — that institutions are what they are because men are what they are.
Secrets and self-presentation — there's a thread running from the beadle to the drawing rooms of Chesney Wold.
James, I want to bring you to a very different kind of revelation — Bucket's unmasking of Hortense before Sir Leicester.
In a novel saturated with hidden identities, how does that scene land for you?
It's one of the most efficiently brutal moments in the entire novel.
Bucket has had Hortense living under his roof for weeks — his own lodger, his domestic guest — while gathering evidence against her.
And he introduces her to Sir Leicester with absolute casualness —
"This is my lodger, Sir Leicester Dedlock. This foreign young woman has been my lodger for some weeks back."
The repetition of lodger is everything — flat, deliberate, merciless.
Bucket is dismantling her with a single word, repeated twice.
He's not accusing — he's classifying.
And in Victorian England, classification was its own form of verdict.
The word foreign does an enormous amount of work in that sentence too.
Bucket doesn't say maid, doesn't say suspect, doesn't say dangerous.
He says foreign — and for Sir Leicester Dedlock, baronet, with all his ancestral furniture of assumption, that carries its own charge.
When I read Bucket aloud, I always try to find that quality of absolute stillness beneath the surface movement.
He's the most dangerous character in the book precisely because he is comfortable everywhere and gives nothing away.
Bucket is, I think, the most modern character Dickens ever created.
He is professional in the sense we now use the word — meaning that he has no private self to compromise his function.
That is, in its way, as troubling as anything Chancery does.
At least Chancery is incompetent.
I want to come back, briefly, to a passage Edmund touched on earlier — the Skimpole daughters.
It seems slight on the page — the daughters laughing at their father's self-characterisation.
But in the context of everything we've been discussing — secrets, complicity, vanity — does it land differently?
It's the Comedy daughter who particularly amuses Dickens — and Dickens who particularly amuses us by naming her so.
Arethusa, Laura, Kitty — the three Skimpole daughters, categorised by their father as Sentiment, Beauty, and Comedy.
It's a perfect Skimpolian act — reducing his children to ornamental functions.
And then Dickens gives us this: the daughters appeared to be very fond of him, amused by this droll fact.
"The daughters, who appeared to be very fond of him, were amused by this droll fact, particularly the Comedy daughter."
Particularly the Comedy daughter — it's so perfectly placed.
The joke names itself.
What disturbs me rather more than the comedy is the fondness.
They appeared to be very fond of him — Dickens doesn't say they were.
Appeared is doing quiet, devastating work in that sentence.
These children have been so thoroughly formed by Skimpole's theatre of himself that they have learned to perform affection for an audience.
That is not comic — or not only comic.
That is the quiet damage wrought by a man who made vanity into a philosophy of life.
There's a Snagsby parallel worth drawing here — different register entirely, but the same mechanism.
Snagsby, you'll recall, gives half a crown to Jo — a small, genuine act of human decency.
But when he tells the story, he omits it — again and again, he suppresses the half-crown fact.
Dickens gives us the exact phrasing twice: suppressing the half-crown fact.
"And Mr. Snagsby again relates his experience, again suppressing the half-crown fact."
The repetition is the story — the compulsive, anxious, self-protective suppression.
Snagsby fears his wife.
But the novel is asking us to consider what it costs — to a man and to a child — when small decencies are hidden because the social cost of owning them is too high.
The half-crown is one of those Dickensian details that seems trivial and is absolutely not.
Snagsby has a good heart — Dickens never lets us forget that.
And yet that good heart operates entirely in secret, because the world around him has made kindness into a liability.
The beadle wants to be seen too much.
Snagsby cannot afford to be seen at all.
Dickens holds those two men in the same hand, and lets us feel the weight of both.
Which is, in the end, what I mean when I speak of moral imagination.
Dickens does not ask us to admire a system or despise another.
He asks us to feel what it is to be Snagsby — well-meaning, frightened, complicit in the smallest possible way.
And then to ask ourselves whether we would do any differently.
Edmund, James, Oliver — this has been a conversation I suspect none of us wanted to end.
Bleak House is a novel that rewards exactly this kind of attention — the close look, the second thought, the willingness to sit with what makes us uncomfortable.

Whether you come to it as Edmund does, with faith in the novel's moral imagination, or as James does, with the historian's eye for what those institutions actually cost — or with Oliver's performer's ear for the music of the prose —
Bleak House endures because it is telling the truth about us.
Not about Victorian England — about us.
Thank you for joining us on Bleak House Unpacked.
We'll be back next week with another deep reading of the novel that refuses, as Dickens himself might say, to be disposed of by any act of parliament.

down again with an impatient laugh and beating the devil’s tattoo
with his boot on the patternless carpet.

thought it a good opportunity to come to the subject of my visit and
to attract Mrs. Jellyby’s attention.

c63:p44.text: The ironmaster, repressing his amused smile, assents.
c63:p44.summary: Rouncewell agrees with amusement to describe George this way.

c20:p123.text:
But fashion is Mr. Weevle’s, as it was Tony Jobling’s, weakness. To
borrow yesterday’s paper from the Sol’s Arms of an evening and read
about the brilliant and distinguished meteors that are shooting
across the fashionable sky in every direction is unspeakable
consolation to him. To know what member of what brilliant and
distinguished circle accomplished the brilliant and distinguished
feat of joining it yesterday or contemplates the no less brilliant
and distinguished feat of leaving it to-morrow gives him a thrill of
joy. To be informed what the Galaxy Gallery of British Beauty is
about, and means to be about, and what Galaxy marriages are on the
tapis, and what Galaxy rumours are in circulation, is to become
acquainted with the most glorious destinies of mankind. Mr. Weevle
reverts from this intelligence to the Galaxy portraits implicated,
and seems to know the originals, and to be known of them.
c20:p123.summary: Weevle reads fashion news about the Galaxy Gallery of British Beauty with rapt attention, deriving his greatest joy from tracking fashionable marriages and scandals.

c26:p129.text:
“Everything concerns me that has a chance in it of bringing anything
to light about him. Didn’t he take us all in? Didn’t he owe us
immense sums, all round? Concern me? Who can anything about him
concern more than me? Not, my dear friend,” says Grandfather
Smallweed, lowering his tone, “that I want YOU to betray anything.
Far from it. Are you ready to come, my dear friend?”
c26:p129.summary: Smallweed explains that Captain Hawdon owes him money and many others, hence his interest, while assuring George he doesn't expect betrayal.

c34:p39.text:
“George,” says that old girl, “I wonder at you! George, I am ashamed
of you! George, I couldn’t have believed you would have done it! I
always knew you to be a rolling stone that gathered no moss, but I
never thought you would have taken away what little moss there was
for Bagnet and the children to lie upon. You know what a
hard-working, steady-going chap he is. You know what Quebec and Malta
and Woolwich are, and I never did think you would, or could, have had
the heart to serve us so. Oh, George!” Mrs. Bagnet gathers up her
cloak to wipe her eyes on in a very genuine manner, “How could you do
it?”
c34:p39.summary: Mrs. Bagnet expands her accusation, comparing George to a rolling stone that has stolen even the little security the family had, and weeps over his betrayal.

c40:p96.text:
“The captain in the army being dead, she believed herself safe; but a
train of circumstances with which I need not trouble you led to
discovery. As I received the story, they began in an imprudence on
her own part one day when she was taken by surprise, which shows how
difficult it is for the firmest of us (she was very firm) to be
always guarded. There was great domestic trouble and amazement, you
may suppose; I leave you to imagine, Sir Leicester, the husband’s
grief. But that is not the present point. When Mr. Rouncewell’s
townsman heard of the disclosure, he no more allowed the girl to be
patronized and honoured than he would have suffered her to be trodden
underfoot before his eyes. Such was his pride, that he indignantly
took her away, as if from reproach and disgrace. He had no sense of
the honour done him and his daughter by the lady’s condescension; not
the least. He resented the girl’s position, as if the lady had been
the commonest of commoners. That is the story. I hope Lady Dedlock
will excuse its painful nature.”
c40:p96.summary: The captain being dead, the secret was exposed through the lady's imprudence. The working-class man learned of his daughter's patronage and angrily withdrew her, refusing aristocratic condescension.
c40:p96.best_quote: Such was his pride, that he indignantly took her away, as if from reproach and disgrace. He had no sense of the honour done him and his daughter by the lady's condescension; not the least. He resented the girl's position, as if the lady had been the commonest of commoners.

c39:p7.text:
The Chancellor is, within these ten minutes, “up” for the long
vacation. Mr. Vholes, and his young client, and several blue bags
hastily stuffed out of all regularity of form, as the larger sort of
serpents are in their first gorged state, have returned to the
official den. Mr. Vholes, quiet and unmoved, as a man of so much
respectability ought to be, takes off his close black gloves as if he
were skinning his hands, lifts off his tight hat as if he were
scalping himself, and sits down at his desk. The client throws his
hat and gloves upon the ground—tosses them anywhere, without looking
after them or caring where they go; flings himself into a chair, half
sighing and half groaning; rests his aching head upon his hand and
looks the portrait of young despair.
c39:p7.summary: The Chancellor has risen for vacation; Vholes and his young client Richard Carstone return to the office. Vholes is impassive while Richard throws himself into a chair in evident despair.

c32:p61.text:
“Forgotten? Trust him for that. He never forgets anything. I saw him
to-night, about eight—helped him to shut up his shop—and he had got
the letters then in his hairy cap. He pulled it off and showed ’em
me. When the shop was closed, he took them out of his cap, hung his
cap on the chair-back, and stood turning them over before the fire. I
heard him a little while afterwards, through the floor here, humming
like the wind, the only song he knows—about Bibo, and old Charon,
and Bibo being drunk when he died, or something or other. He has been
as quiet since as an old rat asleep in his hole.”
c32:p61.summary: Weevle confirms Krook will not forget, recounting how he saw him earlier with the letters displayed in his hairy cap, then later humming a song about death and drunkenness before falling mysteriously quiet.
c32:p61.best_quote: humming like the wind, the only song he knows—about Bibo, and old Charon, and Bibo being drunk when he died

c45:p85.text:

only an instantaneous emotion. I turned my head aside, and it was
gone.
c45:p85.summary: Esther blushes involuntarily but recovers her composure quickly.

c55:p3.text:
“Why, George,” returns Mrs. Bagnet, “was always free with me, ma’am,
and when he said at our house to my Woolwich that of all the things
my Woolwich could have to think of when he grew to be a man, the
comfortablest would be that he had never brought a sorrowful line
into his mother’s face or turned a hair of her head grey, then I felt
sure, from his way, that something fresh had brought his own mother
into his mind. I had often known him say to me, in past times, that
he had behaved bad to her.”
c55:p3.summary: Mrs. Bagnet recounts how George revealed his longing for his mother through his advice to her son Woolwich.

to Ada and Richard.

c31:p21.text:

closely in one another as she stood looking at me that I had no great

c53:p1.text:
Otherwise mildly studious in his observation of human nature, on the
whole a benignant philosopher not disposed to be severe upon the
follies of mankind, Mr. Bucket pervades a vast number of houses and
strolls about an infinity of streets, to outward appearance rather
languishing for want of an object. He is in the friendliest condition
towards his species and will drink with most of them. He is free with
his money, affable in his manners, innocent in his conversation—but
through the placid stream of his life there glides an under-current
of forefinger.
c53:p1.summary: Mr. Bucket appears mild and philosophical but is driven by an undercurrent of investigative purpose as he mingles with society.

c39:p38.text:
“Mr. C.,” returns Vholes, “I wish to say no more of any third party
than is necessary. I wish to leave my good name unsullied, together
with any little property of which I may become possessed through
industry and perseverance, to my daughters Emma, Jane, and Caroline.
I also desire to live in amity with my professional brethren. When
Mr. Skimpole did me the honour, sir—I will not say the very high
honour, for I never stoop to flattery—of bringing us together in
this room, I mentioned to you that I could offer no opinion or advice
as to your interests while those interests were entrusted to another
member of the profession. And I spoke in such terms as I was bound to
speak of Kenge and Carboy’s office, which stands high. You, sir,
thought fit to withdraw your interests from that keeping nevertheless
and to offer them to me. You brought them with clean hands, sir, and
I accepted them with clean hands. Those interests are now paramount
in this office. My digestive functions, as you may have heard me
mention, are not in a good state, and rest might improve them; but I
shall not rest, sir, while I am your representative. Whenever you
want me, you will find me here. Summon me anywhere, and I will come.
During the long vacation, sir, I shall devote my leisure to studying
your interests more and more closely and to making arrangements for
moving heaven and earth (including, of course, the Chancellor) after
Michaelmas term; and when I ultimately congratulate you, sir,” says
Mr. Vholes with the severity of a determined man, “when I ultimately
congratulate you, sir, with all my heart, on your accession to
fortune—which, but that I never give hopes, I might say something
further about—you will owe me nothing beyond whatever little balance
may be then outstanding of the costs as between solicitor and client
not included in the taxed costs allowed out of the estate. I pretend
to no claim upon you, Mr. C., but for the zealous and active
discharge—not the languid and routine discharge, sir: that much
credit I stipulate for—of my professional duty. My duty prosperously
ended, all between us is ended.”
c39:p38.summary: Vholes delivers a lengthy profession of principles: commitment to Richard's interests, moral rectitude toward third parties, professional etiquette, and single-minded devotion despite personal suffering. His daughters Emma, Jane, and Caroline are named as his future beneficiaries.
c39:p38.best_quote: Those interests are now paramount in this office. My digestive functions, as you may have heard me mention, are not in a good state, and rest might improve them; but I shall not rest, sir, while I am your representative.

c51:p23.text:

for my part of it.”

down on his knees before her. Whether in a late repentance, whether
in the first association that comes back upon him, he puts his hands
together as a child does when it says its prayers, and raising them
towards her breast, bows down his head, and cries.

c12:p36.text:
That evening, in the housekeeper’s room, Rosa can do nothing but
murmur Lady Dedlock’s praises. She is so affable, so graceful, so
beautiful, so elegant; has such a sweet voice and such a thrilling
touch that Rosa can feel it yet! Mrs. Rouncewell confirms all this,
not without personal pride, reserving only the one point of
affability. Mrs. Rouncewell is not quite sure as to that. Heaven
forbid that she should say a syllable in dispraise of any member of
that excellent family, above all, of my Lady, whom the whole world
admires; but if my Lady would only be “a little more free,” not quite
so cold and distant, Mrs. Rouncewell thinks she would be more
affable.
c12:p36.summary: That evening, Rosa praises Lady Dedlock effusively; Mrs. Rouncewell confirms most of this but privately feels Lady Dedlock could be warmer and more affable.

c20:p7.text:
“Why, you don’t mean it!” says Mr. Guppy, aroused. “Small! Here’s
Jobling!” Small’s head looks out of window too and nods to Jobling.
c20:p7.summary: Guppy excitedly recognizes Jobling; Smallweed nods greeting from the window.

c11:p70.text:
So they go out in a loose procession, something after the manner of a
straggling funeral, and make their inspection in Mr. Krook’s back
second floor, from which a few of the jurymen retire pale and
precipitately. The beadle is very careful that two gentlemen not very
neat about the cuffs and buttons (for whose accommodation he has
provided a special little table near the coroner in the Harmonic
Meeting Room) should see all that is to be seen. For they are the
public chroniclers of such inquiries by the line; and he is not
superior to the universal human infirmity, but hopes to read in print
what “Mooney, the active and intelligent beadle of the district,”
said and did and even aspires to see the name of Mooney as familiarly
and patronizingly mentioned as the name of the hangman is, according
to the latest examples.
c11:p70.summary: The jury view the body in Krook's back room; the beadle ensures newspaper reporters have a good view and hopes for favorable mention in print.
c11:p70.best_quote: for whose accommodation he has provided a special little table near the coroner in the Harmonic Meeting Room

c54:p96.text:
“This is my lodger, Sir Leicester Dedlock,” says Mr. Bucket, nodding
at her. “This foreign young woman has been my lodger for some weeks
back.”
c54:p96.summary: Bucket identifies Hortense to Sir Leicester as his lodger of several weeks.

c43:p53.text:
The daughters, who appeared to be very fond of him, were amused by
this droll fact, particularly the Comedy daughter.
c43:p53.summary: The daughters laugh at their father's characterization, especially Kitty.

c19:p62.text:
“It was very good-natured of you, sir,” says Mr. Snagsby, “and I am
obliged to you.” And Mr. Snagsby again relates his experience, again
suppressing the half-crown fact.
c19:p62.summary: Mr. Snagsby expresses gratitude and repeats his account of Jo, again omitting the half-crown.
